questions.q: Why do real databases split data across multiple tables instead of one giant table?
options: It's a legacy limitation with no real benefit today
Data is normalized into focused tables, each representing one kind of thing
Multiple tables are only used for very small databases
SQL Server has a hard limit of 20 columns per table
questions.explain: This is deliberate design (normalization), covered formally in Chapter 11 — not disorganization.

questions.q: What does a primary key guarantee?
options: It links to a foreign key in the same table
It must always be a text column
It uniquely identifies each row in a table, and cannot be NULL
It determines the sort order of query results automatically
questions.explain: No two rows can share a primary key value, and it can never be NULL.

options: A column that can never be indexed
A key used only for encryption
A primary key that belongs to a different database entirely
A column in one table that references a primary key in another table
questions.explain: In the example, Sales.SalesOrderDetail.ProductID is a foreign key pointing at Production.Product.ProductID.

questions.q: In the example, what does Sales.SalesOrderDetail.ProductID represent?
options: A link to a specific row in Production.Product, saying which product this order line refers to
The total quantity of a product in stock
A duplicate copy of the product's own primary key definition
An unrelated column with the same name by coincidence
questions.explain: Shared column names across tables like this are exactly what a JOIN condition connects.

questions.q: What does a JOIN (covered starting next lesson) fundamentally do?
options: Combines rows from more than one table based on a shared/related column
Sorts a single table by multiple columns
Merges two tables permanently into one on disk
Deletes rows that don't match a condition
questions.explain: JOIN answers questions that require data from more than one table at once, like 'what did this customer buy?'
